blocks.text: We will treat each instrument or device individually in the order you listed, covering identification, labelling, classification, principles, indications, advantages, disadvantages, complications, clinical applications, and high-yield OSCE viva questions.

A feeding tube is a flexible hollow medical device inserted into the gastrointestinal tract to deliver nutrition, fluids, and sometimes medications to patients who cannot meet their nutritional requirements safely or adequately by mouth.
Depending on its type, it may be introduced through the nose, mouth, abdominal wall, or directly into the small intestine.

Important distinction: A feeding tube is a broad category of devices. A Ryle's tube is one particular type of nasogastric tube, traditionally used for gastric aspiration and decompression as well as feeding in suitable circumstances.
Expected identification: Feeding tube, commonly a nasogastric or enteral feeding tube.
Long, narrow, flexible tube.
Hollow lumen for delivery of feeds.
Graduated markings indicating insertion depth.
Proximal connector for a feeding syringe or enteral giving set.
Distal opening and, depending on the design, additional side holes.
Some models have a guidewire or stylet to facilitate insertion.
In an OSCE, identify the specific tube displayed rather than assuming that every feeding tube is nasogastric.

blocks.text: Safety point: Enteral feeding connectors should be compatible with enteral systems, such as ENFit where applicable, to reduce misconnections with intravenous lines.
Passed through the nose into the stomach.
Used for short-term gastric feeding, medication administration, and, for appropriate tube types, aspiration or decompression.
Passed through the nose, stomach, and pylorus into the jejunum.
Used when post-pyloric feeding is indicated, such as in selected patients with impaired gastric emptying or high aspiration risk.

Examples include PEG tubes and surgically placed gastrostomy tubes. Used when longer-term gastric feeding is required.
Enters the jejunum, usually through the abdominal wall.
Used for longer-term post-pyloric feeding in selected patients, including some patients following upper gastrointestinal surgery.
Other classifications include small-bore versus large-bore tubes, short-term versus long-term devices, and tubes made from polyurethane, silicone, or other medical-grade materials.
Feeding tubes work by providing an artificial route for delivering nutrients into the gastrointestinal tract.
Enteral nutrition: Formula enters the stomach or small intestine and is absorbed through the gut.
Bolus feeding: A prescribed volume is delivered intermittently.
Intermittent feeding: Feed is administered at scheduled intervals.
Continuous feeding: A pump delivers feed at a prescribed rate.
Medication administration: Certain suitable formulations can be administered through a compatible tube after checking suitability and flushing requirements.
The choice of tube and feeding regimen depends on gastrointestinal function, expected duration of support, aspiration risk, nutritional requirements, and the patient's clinical condition.
Common indications include:
Dysphagia following stroke or neurological disease, when enteral feeding is appropriate.
Reduced consciousness or inability to swallow safely.
Head and neck cancers or other conditions that impair oral intake.
Severe illness associated with inadequate oral intake.
Nutritional support in selected patients following major surgery.
Gastric or intestinal feeding when the chosen route is clinically appropriate.
Medication administration when oral administration is not possible and the medication is suitable for tube delivery.
A feeding tube should not be inserted solely because a patient is unwell; the indication, expected duration, goals of care, and risks should be assessed.

Gastrostomy and jejunostomy placement involve procedural risks beyond those of simple nasal tube insertion.
A nasogastric tube may enter the respiratory tract instead of the oesophagus. Feeding through a misplaced tube can cause severe aspiration, pneumonitis, respiratory failure, or death.
Feed or gastric contents enter the airway, particularly in patients with impaired swallowing, reflux, or reduced consciousness.
Nasal irritation, epistaxis, sore throat, oesophageal injury, or pressure injury around the fixation site.
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension, diarrhoea, constipation, tube blockage, and feed intolerance.
Dehydration, electrolyte disturbances, hyperglycaemia, and refeeding syndrome in susceptible malnourished patients.
Additional complications of gastrostomy or jejunostomy tubes include infection at the insertion site, leakage, bleeding, peritonitis, and accidental displacement.
Contraindications depend on the route and type of tube.
Nasogastric tube precautions include:
Suspected basilar skull fracture or severe midface trauma: avoid blind nasal insertion.
Suspected oesophageal obstruction, perforation, or major injury.
Oesophageal varices, recent upper gastrointestinal surgery, or significant bleeding risk: seek appropriate specialist assessment before insertion.
Reduced consciousness or impaired airway protection: assess airway safety and aspiration risk.
A different route, guided placement, or specialist assistance may be required.

subsections.subsection_title: OSCE procedure: nasogastric feeding tube insertion

blocks.text: This is the usual practical station when an examiner presents a feeding tube and asks you to demonstrate its insertion. Actual placement must follow local protocols and supervised clinical training.
Preparation: Confirm the indication, review contraindications, explain the procedure, obtain consent, perform hand hygiene, and assemble the correct tube and equipment.
Positioning: Sit the patient upright where possible, assess the nostrils, and select the more patent nostril.
Measurement: Estimate the required insertion length using the locally approved method. Document the external reference point.
Insertion: Lubricate with a suitable water-soluble lubricant and advance gently according to the tube's instructions. Never force the tube against resistance.
Patient monitoring: Observe for respiratory distress, persistent coughing, cyanosis, or other signs of respiratory placement. Stop and reassess if concerning symptoms occur.
Securement: Fix the tube appropriately and document its external length.
Position confirmation: Confirm the tube's position using the approved local protocol before administering feed, water, or medication.
Documentation: Record the indication, tube type and size, insertion details, external length, confirmation method and result, and any complications.

content_groups.group_title: Critical safety point: confirming tube position

blocks.text: Do not use the air-bolus auscultation test — listening over the stomach after injecting air does not reliably confirm gastric placement.
For a newly inserted nasogastric tube, accepted confirmation methods generally include appropriately interpreted aspirate pH testing and/or radiography, according to the local protocol.
If aspirate cannot be obtained, the pH is outside the locally accepted range, or the result is uncertain, do not use the tube until placement has been confirmed by the approved method.
Radiographs must be interpreted by a competent clinician using the relevant anatomical criteria.
Recheck for displacement according to local policy before subsequent use and whenever displacement is suspected.
Q1. What is the difference between a feeding tube and a Ryle's tube?

A feeding tube is a general term for devices used to deliver enteral nutrition. A Ryle's tube is a type of nasogastric tube, traditionally a larger-bore tube used for gastric aspiration, decompression, and other appropriate indications. Fine-bore tubes are commonly preferred for routine enteral feeding.
Q2. How do you confirm correct placement of a nasogastric tube?
By the approved local protocol, commonly pH testing of aspirate and/or radiography. Air-bolus auscultation is unreliable and must not be used as confirmation.
Q3. What is the most dangerous complication?
Respiratory tract misplacement followed by administration of feed, which can result in severe pulmonary injury or death.
Q4. When would you choose a gastrostomy instead of an NG tube?
When longer-term enteral feeding is expected and gastrostomy is clinically appropriate, after considering prognosis, procedural risks, patient preferences, and the goals of care.
Q5. What is refeeding syndrome?

A potentially fatal metabolic disturbance that can occur when nutrition is reintroduced to a severely malnourished patient. Hypophosphataemia is characteristic; hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, fluid shifts, and thiamine deficiency may also occur.
Q6. What would you do if the tube becomes blocked?
Stop feeding, assess the tube and patient, and follow the approved flushing and troubleshooting protocol. Do not force fluid through the tube or use unapproved methods to unblock it.
Identification: State the exact device and route rather than simply saying “a tube.”
Labelling: Point out the proximal connector, shaft, graduated markings, distal tip, and side holes where present.
Safety: Never feed through a newly inserted NG tube before confirmation of its position.
Clinical reasoning: Choose gastric versus post-pyloric feeding according to the patient's clinical needs.
Complications: Prioritise respiratory misplacement, aspiration, blockage, displacement, and refeeding syndrome.
Communication: Always mention consent, patient comfort, infection prevention, documentation, and ongoing monitoring.
Model OSCE presentation:

“This is an enteral feeding tube, most likely a nasogastric feeding tube. It is a flexible hollow tube used to deliver nutrition, fluids, and suitable medications into the gastrointestinal tract. Its identifiable parts include the proximal connector, graduated shaft, and distal tip with side holes where present. Indications include inadequate or unsafe oral intake when enteral nutrition is appropriate. Complications include misplacement, aspiration, nasal trauma, blockage, displacement, and metabolic disturbances. Correct position must be confirmed according to the approved protocol before the tube is used.”
